source.title: Évaluation de la robustesse des modèles de fondation pour la détection de deepfakes audio : Influence de la diversité linguistique des données de pré-entraînement
source.authors: H. Tran; Damien Lolive; Aghilas Sini; David Guennec; A. Delhay; P. Marteau

record.tranche_reason: The study compares foundation-model sizes on a downstream task and reports that performance gains from increasing size are neither systematic nor proportional. It does not fit or test language-model pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream audio deepfake-detection EERs for models with different sizes and pretraining configurations. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss, training tokens or compute, fit scaling laws, or determine a compute-optimal allocation. Its comparison of languages and model sizes is not itself evidence for a power law.
record.test_reason: Fine-tuned speech foundation models of several sizes within the same families (HuBERT Base/Large/XL; XLS-R-128 0.3B/1B/2B; MMS and Omnilingual 0.3B/1B) are compared on downstream deepfake-detection EER. That gives a downstream-scaling result for V6 in a speech setting. Coverage is about one order of magnitude of size, uses public checkpoints, involves no loss and no fit, and size is confounded with pretraining data.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that multilingual SFMs systematically beat monolingual ones, even ones with more parameters, and that scaling beyond 1B gives marginal gains. Linguistic diversity of pretraining data matters more than raw capacity. Within monolingual families, size gains are moderate and neither systematic nor proportional.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes speech foundation models for audio deepfake detection and measures EER. It does not use language-model loss scaling-law fits or compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies substantially across evaluation datasets; the authors report poorer generalization on out-of-domain ITW for monolingual models and stronger results for multilingual models.

fits_no_version.finding: Multilingual pretrained speech encoders beat monolingual ones on all benchmarks, even monolingual models of similar or larger size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining data diversity, not parameter count, drives downstream robustness of fine-tuned speech encoders.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. Model size and pretraining configuration vary together, so the comparisons do not isolate parameter count as the cause of differences. The study evaluates EER rather than loss and does not fit a predictive scaling relation.
record.rows_left_out: Kept all 19LA-Eval and ITW entries from Table 1 and selected 14 of the 21LA and 21DF entries to stay within the 60-row limit. The other 21LA and 21DF model-by-dataset results in Table 1 are omitted.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss and no power-law fits.
No power-law form is fitted for speech pretraining or fine-tuning.
No predictability from pretraining loss. No language-model tasks. No fitted trend. Only about one order of magnitude of size (Base to 2B).

record.verdict_notes: Off-domain for this claim: speech SSL encoders fine-tuned for classification, not language-model pretraining. The evidence is a set of public checkpoints spanning about 0.1B to 2B, where size changes together with pretraining data. There are no error bars and single runs. The 21LA/21DF values for multilingual models (e.g. XLS-R-128 21DF: 0.3B 1.46, 1B 1.68, 2B 1.53; MMS 2.79 to 2.08; Omnilingual 3.13 to 2.63) are omitted rows, declared in rows_left_out; they follow the same family pattern. Base rows act as baselines; their states stay cannot_determine. Kaplan et al. is cited only in passing, for TTS.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss or power-law fits in parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation experiment or parameter/token allocation fits.
No controlled comparison of depth, width or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The study evaluates fine-tuned speech foundation models, but does not test whether a power-law form holds in speech or other training regimes.
Tests parameter-scale-related downstream performance in audio deepfake detection; does not test language-model downstream tasks or predictability from pretraining loss.
No scaling exponents or compute-optimal split are fitted, and no fitting-method sensitivity is tested.

relationships.condition: Monolingual Base to Large and MMS/Omnilingual 0.3B to 1B, fine-tuned speech encoders, deepfake-detection EER
relationships.reason: Larger models usually lower EER (19A10, 19A12, 21LA02, 21DF06, ITW21, ITW22), but gains are small on ITW (ITW08, ITW10, ITW12). Size is confounded with pretraining data.
relationships.display_finding: Larger models generally reduced equal error rate, but ITW gains were small and size comparisons were confounded by pretraining data.

relationships.condition: XLS-R-128 0.3B to 1B to 2B; HuBERT Large to XL; Voxpopuli Base to Large; wav2vec 2.0 on 21DF
relationships.reason: Larger variants have higher EER than smaller siblings (19A20, ITW20, 19A13, 19A09, ITW09, 21DF02). Authors call 2B gains non-systematic.
relationships.display_finding: Larger variants had higher equal error rates than smaller siblings in the tested comparisons, and gains at 2B were inconsistent.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Compared model-size variants on the evaluated audio deepfake-detection benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: The authors state that increasing model size gives only moderate gains and is neither systematic nor proportional; larger variants can match or underperform smaller ones, and 2B scale gives no systematic ITW gain. See the size comparisons in the linked rows.
